thracian_kotys.name: purifies initiates through ritual immersion
thracian_kotys.notes: Her devotees were called baptai ('dippers') from the ritual washings of her nocturnal rites.

sources.reference: Juvenal, Satires 2.91-92

thracian_pleistoros.name: grants victory in war to those who sacrifice captives to him
thracian_pleistoros.notes: Inferred war-god function: the Apsinthian Thracians sacrificed the captured Persian general Oeobazus to him.

sources.reference: Herodotus, Histories 9.119

thracian_rhesus.name: would have been invincible had he and his horses drunk and grazed at Troy
thracian_rhesus.notes: Oracle-version motif: if Rhesus' snow-white horses drank from the Scamander and ate Trojan grass, he would be unconquerable; hence his slaying on the first night.

sources.reference: scholia to Homer, Iliad 10.435; Euripides (attrib.), Rhesus

thracian_rhesus.name: prophesies underground as a man-daemon of the Bistonian mines
thracian_rhesus.notes: His goddess-mother foretells he will dwell in the silver-bearing caverns of Pangaeum as an anthropodaimon, giving oracles.

sources.reference: Euripides (attrib.), Rhesus 962-973

thracian_zibelthiurdos.name: sends the rain as lord of the storm-sky
thracian_zibelthiurdos.notes: His name is read as 'thunderer' / 'lightning-bearer'; the Thracian reflex of the Indo-European sky-storm god.

sources.reference: D. Detschew, Die thrakischen Sprachreste (s.v. Zbelsurdos)

thracian_semele.name: is the earth from which life springs
thracian_semele.notes: Thraco-Phrygian Zemelo, 'mother earth'; a Phrygian inscription pairs her as dios zemelo ('to Zeus and to the Earth').

sources.reference: J. Pokorny, Indogermanisches etymologisches Worterbuch (root *dheghom)

tinguian_kadaklan.name: makes thunder by beating his great drum in the sky
tinguian_kadaklan.notes: Thunder is Kadaklan amusing himself on his drum during storms, and sometimes on clear days.

sources.reference: F.-C. Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915)

tinguian_kadaklan.name: sends his servant Kaboniyan to earth to teach mankind
tinguian_kadaklan.notes: Seeing the people hungry and sick, he dispatches Kaboniyan to teach planting, prayer, curing, and the driving-off of evil spirits.

sources.reference: F.-C. Cole, Traditions of the Tinguian (1915)

tinguian_makaboteng.name: frightens the deer and wild hogs toward or away from the hunters
tinguian_makaboteng.notes: His name means 'one who frightens'; his good will is required for the hunting dogs to succeed.

sources.reference: F.-C. Cole, The Tinguian: Social, Religious, and Economic Life of a Philippine Tribe (1922)

tiv_aondo.name: roars and flashes as thunder and lightning
tiv_aondo.notes: Thunder is 'Aondo kume' (God roars); lightning 'Aondo nyiar' (God flashes); a coming storm is 'Aondo ngu van a ura' (God comes with the storm).

sources.reference: R. C. Abraham, The Tiv People (1933)

tlingit_raven.name: transforms himself to a hemlock needle to be reborn of the sky-chief's daughter
tlingit_raven.notes: To steal the boxes of daylight he becomes a spruce/hemlock needle in the girl's drinking water, is swallowed, and is born as her son.

sources.reference: J. R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)

tlingit_thunderbird.name: flashes lightning from its eyes
tlingit_thunderbird.notes: Thunder comes from the beating of its wings, lightning from the blink/flash of its eyes; the Wrangell firedrake (Kah-lit) is folded into this lightning aspect.

sources.reference: J. R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)

toba_carancho.name: orders the world and fixes the present human condition
toba_carancho.notes: As the principal Toba culture-hero (the caracara), he clears the world of the man-devouring monsters and establishes the order under which people now live.

sources.reference: A. Metraux, Myths of the Toba and Pilaga Indians of the Gran Chaco (1946)

toba_kasogonaga.name: falls from the sky and must be helped by humans to return aloft
toba_kasogonaga.notes: In a widespread Toba tale Kasogonaga (a small hairy/anteater-like or rainbow-elephant being) drops to earth and is restored to the sky by people, thereafter sending rain in gratitude.

sources.reference: A. Metraux, Myths of the Toba and Pilaga Indians of the Gran Chaco (1946)

tongan_ahoeitu.name: climbs the great toa tree to the sky to find his divine father
tongan_ahoeitu.notes: He ascends a toa (ironwood/casuarina) tree connecting earth to the heaven of Tangaloa 'Eitumatupu'a.

sources.reference: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales (1924)

thracian_kotys.name: hand-drums and shrill pipes of the Kotyttia

sources.reference: Strabo, Geography 10.3.16 (quoting Aeschylus, Edonoi)
Philostratus, Heroicus; Lucian, Adversus Indoctum 11

thracian_rhesus.name: armor of gold fit for the gods

sources.reference: Homer, Iliad 10.438-441

sources.reference: P. Kvaerne, The Bon Religion of Tibet (1995)

tlingit_thunderbird.name: world-darkening wings whose beating is thunder

sources.reference: J. R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)

sources.reference: Aeschylus, Edonoi (in Strabo, Geography 10.3.16)
Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 1.34

thracian_sabazios.gloss: the Thracian-Phrygian name behind the ecstatic cry Euoi Saboi

sources.reference: Demosthenes, On the Crown 259-260

thracian_sabazios.gloss: Sabazios identified with Zeus the sky-father

sources.reference: L. E. Roller, In Search of God the Mother / The Anatolian Cult of Sabazios

thracian_rhesus.gloss: man-daemon, midway between mortal and god

sources.reference: Euripides (attrib.), Rhesus 971

thracian_zalmoxis.gloss: the name under which some Getae worship the same god

sources.reference: Herodotus, Histories 4.94

thracian_semele.gloss: the raving one, her divinized name after her son raises her from Hades

sources.reference: Pindar, Pythian 3; Diodorus Siculus 4.25
R. de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet (1956)

sources.reference: R. de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet (1956)

sources.reference: P. Kvaerne, The Bon Religion of Tibet (1995)
R. C. Abraham, The Tiv People (1933)

tlingit_raven.gloss: name of the being who 'made' Raven / Raven-at-the-head-of-Nass

sources.reference: J. R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)

tonga_leza.gloss: the Besetting One, who sends affliction after affliction and never lets you alone

sources.reference: E. W. Smith and A. M. Dale, The Ila-speaking Peoples of Northern Rhodesia (1920)

thracian_kotys.name: the Kotyttia
thracian_kotys.notes: Nocturnal Edonian mountain festival of frenzied drumming and stringed music likened to the rites of Cybele and the Bacchic orgies; celebrants were 'baptai' purified by immersion. Adopted at Athens and Corinth.

sources.reference: Strabo, Geography 10.3.16; Aeschylus, Edonoi

thracian_orpheus.name: oracle of the head of Orpheus on Lesbos
thracian_orpheus.notes: After the maenads tore him apart, his still-singing head floated to Lesbos and gave oracles until silenced by Apollo; Orphic teletai (initiations) of afterlife salvation derive from him.

sources.reference: Philostratus, Heroicus 5; Lucian, Adversus Indoctum 11-12

thracian_pleistoros.name: sacrifice of war-captives to Pleistoros
thracian_pleistoros.notes: The Apsinthians sacrificed the captured Persian Oeobazus to their god Pleistoros.

sources.reference: Herodotus, Histories 9.119

thracian_rhesus.name: Thracian hero-cult of Rhesus
thracian_rhesus.notes: Prophesied in the drama: Rhesus is to be honored as a man-daemon in the silver mines of Thracian Pangaeum, an immortality-without-death paralleling Zalmoxis.

sources.reference: Euripides (attrib.), Rhesus 962-973

thracian_sabazios.name: initiation of Sabazios (the snake through the bosom)
thracian_sabazios.notes: Initiates were purified and a live golden snake ('the god through the bosom', deus per sinum) was drawn down across the body; rites featured night processions and the cry Euoi Saboi.

sources.reference: Demosthenes, On the Crown 259; Clement of Alexandria, Protrepticus 2.16; Arnobius, Adversus Nationes 5.21

thracian_zalmoxis.name: the messenger sent to Zalmoxis
thracian_zalmoxis.notes: Every fifth year the Getae cast a man chosen by lot onto upright spears; if he died he had carried their needs to Zalmoxis, if he lived he was blamed as a bad man.

sources.reference: Herodotus, Histories 4.94

thracian_semele.name: sacrifice to Semele at the Lenaia
thracian_semele.notes: At Athens a yearling bull (emblem of Dionysus, her son) was offered to Semele.

sources.reference: M. P. Nilsson, Greek Popular Religion

tibetan_nyenchen_tanglha.name: incense-smoke offering (sang) to the mountain god
tibetan_nyenchen_tanglha.notes: Mountain god bound by oath by Padmasambhava; honored with morning sang of the three whites and three sweets, juniper incense, alcohol and serkyem libation by herders of the range and pilgrims circuiting Lake Namtso.

sources.reference: R. de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet (1956)

tibetan_pehar.name: the Nechung state oracle
tibetan_pehar.notes: Pehar (through his minister Dorje Drakden) possesses the kuten medium of Nechung monastery, the state oracle consulted by the Tibetan government and the Dalai Lama.

sources.reference: R. de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet (1956)

tibetan_yullha.name: mountain-god cairn worship with arrow-poles
tibetan_yullha.notes: Male worshippers plant arrow-poles (mda' shing) in the lhatse cairn, raise sang smoke, and shout the war-cry 'kyi kyi so so, lha rgyal lo' so that the territorial god may grant crops, herds and victory.

sources.reference: S. G. Karmay, The Arrow and the Spindle

tiv_aondo.name: absence of regular cult (deus otiosus)
tiv_aondo.notes: Aondo created the world and takes no further interest in it; the Tiv address ritual not to him but to the akombo forces and to the ancestors, so he receives no standing cult.

sources.reference: P. Bohannan, The Tiv of Central Nigeria (1953)

tiv_akombo.name: repairing the akombo
tiv_akombo.notes: When an akombo is 'spoiled' it brings the specific sickness it governs; a master of that akombo 'repairs' (soron) it with prescribed sacrifices, medicines and emblems to lift the affliction.

sources.reference: P. Bohannan, The Tiv of Central Nigeria (1953)

tiv_takuruku.name: invocation of the great ancestor at the funeral of an elder
tiv_takuruku.notes: When an old man dies a natural death the ilyu/idyer (drum-horn) is sounded to call Takuruku, father of the Tiv, to come forward and receive his descendant.

sources.reference: Akiga Sai, Akiga's Story: The Tiv Tribe as Seen by One of Its Members (ed. R. East, 1939)

tonga_leza.name: appeal to Leza for rain
tonga_leza.notes: As sky and rain god Leza is invoked for the rains; the myth of the bereaved woman who built a tower of trees to climb to him and failed is the canonical aetiology of human mortality.

sources.reference: E. W. Smith and A. M. Dale, The Ila-speaking Peoples of Northern Rhodesia (1920)

tongan_ahoeitu.name: the royal kava ceremony (taumafa kava)
tongan_ahoeitu.notes: Tradition derives the order of the chiefly kava circle from Tangaloa's kava bowl in which the murderous brothers disgorged 'Aho'eitu's body so he could be revived and installed as first Tu'i Tonga; the brothers became his attendants.

sources.reference: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Society (1929)

attributes.name: singer enthroned amid charmed beasts
attributes.notes: The commonest image: Orpheus seated playing the lyre, surrounded by wild animals, birds, trees and stones drawn to his song; popular on mosaics in late antiquity.

sources.reference: LIMC s.v. Orpheus

attributes.name: Thracian/Phrygian dress and cap
attributes.notes: Marked as a Thracian by his peaked cap and patterned cloak in Attic vase-painting of his death at the maenads' hands.

sources.reference: LIMC s.v. Orpheus

attributes.name: right hand raised in the benedictio (thumb, index, middle extended)
attributes.notes: The signature gesture of the bronze votive Hands of Sabazios, crowded with pine-cone, snake, frog, ram's head and other emblems and mounted on poles for procession.

sources.reference: L. E. Roller, The Anatolian Cult of Sabazios

attributes.name: bearded sky-rider treading a ram's head
attributes.notes: On reliefs (e.g. from Philippopolis) a curly-haired bearded god on horseback, a ram's head beneath his foot, holding a hand-tipped sceptre.

sources.reference: L. E. Roller, The Anatolian Cult of Sabazios
Clement of Alexandria, Protrepticus 2.16

sacredAnimals.name: snow-white horses swifter than the wind

sources.reference: Homer, Iliad 10.436-437

attributes.name: thunderbolt raised in the right hand
attributes.notes: On the votive reliefs he raises a lightning-bolt with an eagle beside him, in the manner of Zeus Keraunios.

sources.reference: D. Detschew, Die thrakischen Sprachreste
D. Detschew, Die thrakischen Sprachreste

attributes.name: deep-blue wrathful body riding side-saddle across a sea of blood
attributes.notes: Three blood-shot eyes, flaming reddish hair crowned with peacock feathers and skulls, a garland of fifty severed heads.

sources.reference: R. de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet (1956)

attributes.name: the mule with an eye on its rump
attributes.notes: Her husband's poisoned arrow wound became a third eye on the mule's haunch; its reins are venomous snakes and the saddle is flayed human skin.

sources.reference: R. de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet (1956)
R. de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet (1956)
R. de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet (1956)

attributes.name: white, three-faced, six-armed king on a snow lion
attributes.notes: White, blue and red faces; six arms bearing hook, arrow, sword, knife, bow and stick; wide-brimmed cane/rattan hat, tiger- and leopard-skin garb.

sources.reference: R. de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet (1956)
R. de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet (1956)

attributes.name: dark-blue buffalo-headed lord of death in flames
attributes.notes: Buffalo head with flaming brows, crown of skulls, brandishing skull-club and noose, standing on a buffalo that mounts a corpse; his sister Yami offers him a skull-cup of blood.

sources.reference: R. de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet (1956)
R. de Nebesky-Wojkowitz, Oracles and Demons of Tibet (1956)

attributes.name: serene teacher enthroned on a lotus
attributes.notes: Depicted Buddha-like, jewel-crowned, in meditation posture on a lotus-and-lion throne, holding or flanked by the yungdrung scepter; iconographically a Bon counterpart of Shakyamuni.

sources.reference: P. Kvaerne, The Bon Religion of Tibet (1995)

attributes.name: white-clad warrior on a white horse
attributes.notes: Territorial mountain gods are typically shown as armored white horsemen with banner and lance; some, like Yarlha Shampo, instead manifest as a white yak breathing snowstorms.

sources.reference: S. G. Karmay, The Arrow and the Spindle
S. G. Karmay, The Arrow and the Spindle

attributes.name: once-white bird turned black escaping through the smoke-hole
attributes.notes: Raven was white until, stealing daylight, he fled up the chimney and was blackened by smoke; he names the Raven (Yeil) moiety and is carved at the base of crest poles.

sources.reference: J. R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)

sacredAnimals.name: raven (his own form and crest of the Yeil moiety)

sources.reference: J. R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)

attributes.name: woman in the moon beating tapa
attributes.notes: Seen seated in the moon with her tapa-board and mallet (ike); patroness of bark-cloth beaters, who invoked her as they worked by moonlight.

sources.reference: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Maui (1910)

attributes.name: long tail bound by a cord
attributes.notes: The ruler of Pulotu bears a great tail; Tangaloa in the sky holds one end of the binding cord and Maui the other in the underworld, lest the land of the living follow the dead.

sources.reference: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales (1924)

attributes.name: sky-being who hurls lightning from its mouth
attributes.notes: Variously described as a small hairy anteater-like creature or a multicolored sky-elephant; its falls and rescues are tied to thunder, rain and the rainbow.

sources.reference: A. Metraux, Myths of the Toba and Pilaga Indians of the Gran Chaco (1946)
A. Metraux, Myths of the Toba and Pilaga Indians of the Gran Chaco (1946)
